Knowledge recorded by Shinnecock elders in 2014

Shadbush / serviceberry

The catalogue links shadbush flowering with the end of frost and preparations for the spring shad run. It remembers the fruit as food and an ingredient in pemmican. The plant is a seasonal sign connecting land, water, and work.1

“Wild pear,” “June berry,” and “serviceberry” are names listed with Amelanchier; the catalogue also discusses cultivated pears separately.1

Places named in the catalogue

Shinnecock residential territories; Shinnecock cemetery; Shinnecock Powwow Grounds; The Point.1

Page references

The Shinnecock Environmental Department compiled this catalogue from elders’ memories and community resource knowledge in 2014. Food and medicine appear here as historical knowledge; safe identification and treatment require current guidance.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF p. 17. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.
